title: From Babel’s Tower to Abram’s Family
summary: Humanity’s united bid for a self-made name ends in confusion and scattering, while Shem’s line narrows to Terah’s household and barren Sarai.
historicalContext: The chapter is set in the generations after the flood, when Noah’s descendants moved down from the highlands into the broad alluvial plain of Shinar, the land later called Babylonia. That region had no building stone, so its people learned to fire clay bricks and bind them with bitumen, and its cities came to be crowned by stepped temple towers. Genesis does not borrow Babylon’s own story of a city founded by the gods; it tells instead of mortals who began building in defiance of God and were stopped. The second half moves through ten generations from Shem to Terah, with ages that shorten markedly after the flood, and closes in Ur of the Chaldees, a wealthy and idolatrous city of southern Mesopotamia (Joshua 24:2). From there Terah’s household travels up the Euphrates to Haran, a crossroads on the route toward Canaan.
literaryContext: Genesis 11 is the hinge between the history of all nations and the history of one chosen family. The Babel account explains the scattering already described in the Table of Nations, so chapter 10 gives the result and 11:1-9 its cause; Peleg, in whose days “the earth was divided” (10:25), links the two. The tower story is built as a mirror: human speech and building in verses 1-4 are answered by divine speech and undoing in verses 6-9, with “the LORD came down” at the centre. The genealogy of Shem then resumes the pattern of Genesis 5, ten generations ending in three sons, and the generations of Terah narrow the focus to Abram, Sarai, and Lot. The chapter ends with a family on the road, a wife without a child, and a death short of Canaan, leaving every reader waiting for the call and promise of chapter 12.
themes: Human pride seeking a name apart from God
The LORD who comes down to judge and to restrain
Scattering as both judgment and mercy
The faithful line preserved from Shem to Abram
Barrenness as the stage for divine promise
Pilgrimage toward the land God will show

outline.title: One Speech and a Self-Made Name
outline.summary: United humanity settles in Shinar and resolves to build a city and a tower that will win them fame and keep them together.

outline.title: The LORD Comes Down to Babel
outline.summary: God inspects the work, confounds their language, and scatters them, leaving the unfinished city with the name Babel.

outline.title: The Generations of Shem
outline.summary: Ten generations trace the line of promise from Shem to Terah, with lifespans steadily shortening after the flood.

outline.title: The Household of Terah
outline.summary: Terah’s family is introduced, Sarai’s barrenness is stated, and the household moves from Ur to Haran, where Terah dies.

verses.bibleText: And the whole earth was of one language, and of one speech.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Genesis turns from the orderly Table of Nations to a single episode that explains how those nations came to be spread across the earth. Chapter 10 has already spoken of peoples divided “after their tongues” (10:5, 20, 31). Here the narrator steps back to the cause. The arrangement is deliberate: the result is listed first, and the story that produced it follows, so the reader meets the scattered world before learning why it was scattered.

“The whole earth” refers to the whole human population, still a single company descended from Noah’s three sons and living within a few generations of the flood. They shared “one language, and of one speech.” The two phrases are not idle repetition. The first describes a common tongue; the second points to a shared stock of words and expressions. Nothing separated them in sound, vocabulary, or meaning. Such a unity had real potential for good. One family speaking with one voice could have carried the knowledge of the Creator and the memory of His mercy in the ark to every land they settled.

Even so, the verse carries a warning, because Genesis has already shown what united human purpose becomes when it is cut loose from God. Before the flood the earth was “filled with violence” (6:11). The same capacity for cooperation that might have served God’s command to “replenish the earth” (9:1) is about to be turned against it. Unity is never neutral in Scripture; its value depends on what people are united around.

The chapter will end with the opposite condition: many languages, scattered peoples, and one household beginning a long journey toward Canaan. The God who divided the world’s speech at Babel will later pour out His Spirit so that people “out of every nation under heaven” hear His wonderful works in their own tongues (Acts 2:5-11). The true unity of the human family comes from God’s gift, not from a common project of human pride.

wordNotes.explanation: Literally “one lip.” The lip stands for the speech it forms, as when Isaiah foresees cities in Egypt speaking “the language of Canaan” (literally “lip of Canaan”). The same word returns in verses 6, 7, and 9, framing the story: the single lip of verse 1 becomes the confounded lip of verse 9. Zephaniah’s promise of “a pure language” uses this term for the restored worship of the nations.

Literally “one words” or “the same words.” The plural noun with the plural form of “one” stresses a common vocabulary and manner of expression, beyond a shared grammar. Humanity spoke alike and, as the following verses show, thought alike.

verses.bibleText: And it came to pass, as they journeyed from the east, that they found a plain in the land of Shinar; and they dwelt there.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“As they journeyed” uses a verb that describes pulling up tent pegs and moving camp. After the flood Noah’s descendants lived at first as herders on the move, coming down from the mountains of Ararat (8:4). The KJV’s “from the east” renders a Hebrew expression that elsewhere means “eastward” (2:8; 13:11). Geography favours that sense, since a journey from the Ararat highlands to southern Mesopotamia runs southward and eastward. The rendering also keeps a pattern that runs through Genesis: movement east repeatedly marks departure from the place of blessing. Adam and Eve were driven out at the east of the garden (3:24), Cain went to dwell “on the east of Eden” (4:16), and Lot will later journey east toward Sodom (13:11).

The travellers “found a plain in the land of Shinar.” Shinar is southern Mesopotamia, the region later known as Sumer and Babylonia, already named as the heart of Nimrod’s kingdom (10:10). It was a broad, well-watered, fertile lowland, and its earliest cities show remarkable skill in building, writing, and crafts. To people who had known only mountain slopes, such a plain promised ease and abundance.

Then comes the decisive phrase: “and they dwelt there.” God had told Noah’s sons to multiply and fill the earth (9:1, 7). These settlers chose to stop. Their settling was more than a change of lifestyle; it set the stage for a deliberate resistance to God’s stated purpose. The same verb will describe Terah’s household at the end of the chapter, which also “dwelt there” in Haran (11:31), short of its goal. Between the two settlings the chapter traces two very different responses to God: a people who refuse to move, and a family that God will call to keep moving in faith.

wordNotes.explanation: The expression can mean “from the east” or “in the east, eastward,” depending on context; in Genesis 2:8 the KJV renders it “eastward.” Here the direction of travel from Ararat to Shinar supports “eastward.” In Genesis, eastward movement often accompanies estrangement from God’s presence or promise.

A broad valley or open lowland. The same word describes the plain of Dura in the province of Babylon, where Nebuchadnezzar set up his golden image and demanded that all peoples and languages bow. The two Babylonian plains stand as settings for humanity’s united defiance of God.

verses.bibleText: And they said one to another, Go to, let us make brick, and burn them throughly. And they had brick for stone, and slime had they for morter.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And they said one to another, Go to.” The exclamation “Go to” is the Hebrew havah, a call to action: “Come, let us.” It appears twice from the builders (vv. 3, 4) and once from God (v. 7), and the echo is intentional. The settlers consult only with one another. No altar is built, no name of the LORD is called upon (contrast 4:26; 8:20; 12:8). Their plan begins and ends at the human level.

The narrator pauses over their building materials in a way that would have struck readers in Israel, a land of abundant stone. In the clay plain of Mesopotamia there was no quarry to draw upon, so the settlers learned to mould bricks and fire them “throughly” in kilns, which made them hard and lasting. For mortar they used “slime,” natural bitumen that seeped from the ground in the region and bound brick so firmly that ancient walls still resist separation.

The Hebrew sounds reinforce the scene. “Let us make brick” is literally “let us brick bricks,” and the bitumen and mortar are two near-identical words. The repeated consonants create a pattern of sound as uniform as the brick courses themselves, and as uniform as the single speech of verse 1.

Nothing is wrong with technical skill. Bezalel was filled with the Spirit of God for craftsmanship (Exodus 31:2-5). The danger lies in what the new technology made people feel able to do. With bricks that would not wash away and mortar that would not crack, they could now build higher and more securely than ever. Human ingenuity, lacking any reference to God, quickly becomes the ground of human confidence, and the next verse shows where that confidence led.

wordNotes.term: הָבָה נִלְבְּנָה לְבֵנִים (havah nilbenah levenim) — Go to, let us make brick
wordNotes.explanation: Havah is an interjection urging joint action (“Come!”). Nilbenah levenim is a cognate expression, literally “let us brick bricks.” In verse 7 God answers with the same havah, and His “let us confound” (navlah) uses the same consonants as “let us make brick” in reverse order, a sound-play suggesting that God will undo what they built.

Bitumen or asphalt, a natural petroleum product abundant in Mesopotamia and around the Dead Sea. The same word describes the pits in the vale of Siddim and the waterproofing of the ark of bulrushes. Here it is paired with chomer, “mortar,” in a deliberate play on sound.

verses.bibleText: And they said, Go to, let us build us a city and a tower, whose top may reach unto heaven; and let us make us a name, lest we be scattered abroad upon the face of the whole earth.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The builders now announce their purpose. “Let us build us a city and a tower, whose top may reach unto heaven.” Only once before has Genesis mentioned the building of a city, when Cain, sentenced to be a wanderer, built one and named it after his son (4:17). The settlers of Shinar stand in Cain’s line of thought, even though they descend from Noah. Like him they move east, build a city, and look for security in walls instead of in God.

The tower, migdal, belongs to the family of words for being great. In the setting of Mesopotamia it points to the stepped temple tower, a massive artificial mountain of brick crowned with a shrine, meant to join earth and heaven. To say its top would reach “unto heaven” could describe great height (Deuteronomy 1:28), but here the phrase carries more. Heaven is where God dwells (Psalm 115:16). The builders are reaching for the realm that belongs to Him. Some among them may also have hoped that a structure higher than the flood waters would keep them safe from any future judgment, doubting the promise God had sealed with the rainbow (9:11-15).

“Let us make us a name” lays bare the motive. In Scripture a name stands for reputation, identity, and lasting memory. The builders wanted renown that would outlive them, secured by their own achievement. In the very next chapter God promises Abram, “I will make thy name great” (12:2). The contrast governs the whole passage: a name seized by human effort, or a name received from God.

The final clause exposes their fear: “lest we be scattered abroad upon the face of the whole earth.” What God had commanded as blessing, filling the earth, they regarded as a threat. Pride and anxiety lie side by side in this verse. People who will not trust God must build something to hold their lives together, and the project becomes both a monument to themselves and a fortress against Him. Every generation repeats the pattern, from the boast of Nebuchadnezzar over “great Babylon, that I have built” (Daniel 4:30) to the self-exalting power of the last days that Revelation also calls Babylon (Revelation 14:8). The answer is not to stop building, but to build on the word of God and for His glory.

wordNotes.explanation: A noun related to gadal, “to be great.” Elsewhere it often denotes a fortified watchtower or citadel, and the prophets use it as a symbol of human pride that will be brought low in the day of the LORD. In Mesopotamia it suits the stepped temple tower, an artificial holy mountain.

wordNotes.term: נַעֲשֶׂה־לָּנוּ שֵׁם (na‘aseh-lanu shem) — let us make us a name
wordNotes.explanation: Shem (“name”) means reputation and enduring memory. Making a name is God’s prerogative: He makes a great name for Abram and for David, and makes Himself a glorious name in the exodus. The builders seek by their own hands what God alone gives. The word also echoes Shem, whose genealogy follows in verse 10.

verses.bibleText: And the LORD came down to see the city and the tower, which the children of men builded.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
This short verse is the turning point of the whole account. Everything before it records human speech and human building; everything after it records divine speech and divine action. At the centre stands one sentence: “And the LORD came down.”

The irony is unmistakable. The builders meant their tower to reach heaven, yet the LORD must descend to look at it. However high it rose above the plain, from heaven it was small. Isaiah captures the same perspective when he describes God sitting above the circle of the earth, where its inhabitants look like grasshoppers (Isaiah 40:22). The language of coming down “to see” is spoken in human terms. It does not suggest that God lacked knowledge or had to travel to gain it. The Psalmist says the LORD looks down from heaven upon the children of men and sees all they do (Psalm 33:13-15). The phrase pictures God taking personal notice of human deeds and examining them before He acts. Genesis shows Him doing the same in the garden (3:9-13), with Cain (4:9-10), and later at Sodom: “I will go down now, and see” (18:21). God’s judgments are never hasty. He investigates and then pronounces, so that His justice may be seen to be fair.

The builders are now called “the children of men,” literally “the sons of Adam.” The title reminds the reader what they are: mortal descendants of the man formed from dust, however grand their ambitions. The verb “builded” presents the work as well advanced, though verse 8 will show it was never completed.

The verse also carries hope. Humanity cannot climb to God; God comes down to humanity. That movement, first in judgment here, will become the pattern of redemption. At Sinai God came down to meet His people (Exodus 19:20), and at last the Son of God came down from heaven to give life to the world (John 6:38).

wordNotes.term: וַיֵּרֶד יְהוָה (vayyered YHWH) — and the LORD came down
wordNotes.explanation: The verb yarad, “go down, descend,” is used of God’s personal intervention in human affairs, whether to inspect and judge or to deliver. It answers the builders’ upward reach with a downward movement from heaven. The same verb describes the LORD descending on Sinai and coming down to rescue Israel from Egypt.

wordNotes.term: בְּנֵי הָאָדָם (benei ha’adam) — the children of men
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “sons of the man” or “sons of Adam.” The expression stresses human frailty and creatureliness, often in contrast with God who looks down upon them from heaven. Here it deflates the builders’ heavenly pretensions.

verses.bibleText: And the LORD said, Behold, the people is one, and they have all one language; and this they begin to do: and now nothing will be restrained from them, which they have imagined to do.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The LORD’s assessment is sober. “Behold, the people is one, and they have all one language.” God does not mock the project as a trifle. Their unity of blood and speech gave them extraordinary capacity, and they were turning it toward rebellion. “This they begin to do” marks the tower as a first step. If the work went unchecked, it would set a precedent and open the way to further schemes of the same kind.

The final clause, “nothing will be restrained from them, which they have imagined to do,” is not a compliment to human power. It is a warning about human sin. Before the flood God had seen that “every imagination of the thoughts” of the human heart was “only evil continually” (6:5), and after the flood He acknowledged that this inclination remained (8:21). A humanity united in pride, with no internal check, would quickly ripen in wickedness again. God had promised never again to destroy the earth by a flood (9:11). Here He chooses another way to deal with evil: restraint.

The verse therefore reveals a gracious side to judgment. It is the action of a God who limits evil so that history may continue and redemption may unfold. Throughout Scripture He holds back the full force of evil, setting boundaries even for Satan (Job 1:12; 2:6) and restraining the winds of strife until His servants are sealed (Revelation 7:1). The relative order of human society is itself evidence of that restraining hand.

Job, using the same rare verb, confesses of God, “no thought can be withholden from thee” (Job 42:2). Only of God is it ultimately true that none of His purposes can be thwarted. The builders were grasping at a freedom from all limits that belongs to the Creator alone. Their ambition was the old temptation, “ye shall be as gods” (3:5), expressed now in brick and bitumen.

wordNotes.explanation: From batsar, here in a passive form meaning “to be cut off, withheld, made inaccessible.” The form occurs elsewhere only in Job 42:2, where it describes God, whose purposes cannot be withheld. Applied to humanity, the phrase warns of creatures claiming a limitless power that belongs only to the Creator.

From zamam, “to plan, devise, purpose.” The verb can describe God’s settled purpose, but it is often used of scheming against others. The context shows the builders’ planning as self-directed and opposed to God’s will.

verses.bibleText: Go to, let us go down, and there confound their language, that they may not understand one another's speech.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Go to, let us go down.” God answers the builders in their own words. They had said “Go to, let us make brick” and “Go to, let us build”; now the LORD says “Go to, let us go down.” The mimicry carries a sharp edge. The human “let us” could only stack bricks; the divine “let us” changes reality by a word.

The plural recalls Genesis 1:26, “Let us make man in our image,” and 3:22, “the man is become as one of us.” In each case the God who speaks is one LORD, yet He deliberates within Himself in the plural. The fuller light of Scripture shows a plurality of persons within the one Godhead, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, acting together in creation and in judgment (Matthew 28:19). The LORD who formed humanity by joint counsel now confronts humanity’s joint rebellion. He does not consult the builders, nor does He need angelic advisers; the counsel is His own.

The method is precise. God will “confound their language, that they may not understand one another’s speech.” He does not strike the tower down or send another flood. Toppling the structure would solve nothing, since another could be built. He strikes instead at what made their united defiance possible: shared understanding. When workers cannot understand one another, cooperation ends, mistrust grows, and the project collapses from within.

The confusion was not total chaos in which no one could understand anyone. Groups that could still understand each other drew together and departed together, forming the families and peoples of chapter 10. The judgment set humanity into many communities, so that no single power could easily unite the whole world against God. Rulers have tried ever since to reverse that division by force. The true remedy came from God Himself. At Pentecost the Spirit enabled the apostles to speak so that people of many languages each heard the gospel in their own tongue (Acts 2:6-8). The gospel does not erase the languages; it unites hearers of every tongue in one Lord (Revelation 7:9).

wordNotes.explanation: From balal, “to mix, confuse,” a verb used elsewhere of mixing flour with oil for the meal offering. Here it describes mixing up speech so that meaning is lost. Its consonants n-b-l reverse the l-b-n of “let us make brick” in verse 3, a sound-play showing God unbuilding what the builders made.

verses.bibleText: So the LORD scattered them abroad from thence upon the face of all the earth: and they left off to build the city.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“So the LORD scattered them abroad from thence.” What the builders feared most is exactly what came upon them (v. 4). They had built to avoid being scattered; their building became the occasion of their scattering. The God who had commanded them to fill the earth now ensured that they would, whether they wished to or not. His purpose is not defeated by human resistance. It is accomplished through and in spite of it.

The word “thence,” literally “from there,” answers the “there” of verse 2, where “they dwelt there.” The settled plain becomes the starting point of a dispersal across the world. The narrator does not describe the confusion itself in this verse; he moves straight from God’s intention to its result. Once people could no longer understand one another, scattering followed. Families and clans that shared a tongue moved off together, and within a relatively short span human settlements appeared across the ancient world, from the Nile to the river valleys of Asia.

“And they left off to build the city.” The building stopped. The tower meant to reach heaven stood unfinished, a monument to the limits of human pride. Babylon would later be built and rebuilt into a great city, and its kings would raise towers of their own, but the original enterprise was frustrated at its root. God needed no army and no flood to stop it; the loss of a common tongue was enough.

This act of judgment also carried mercy. By scattering humanity God prevented a unified rebellion from rushing the world toward another universal corruption like that before the flood. The division of peoples became a means of preserving the human race until God’s plan of blessing through Abram’s seed could unfold. Paul told the Athenians that God “hath made of one blood all nations” and determined “the bounds of their habitation,” so that they “should seek the Lord” (Acts 17:26-27). Even scattering was meant to lead people back to God.

wordNotes.explanation: From puts, “to scatter, disperse.” It repeats the builders’ own fear in verse 4 (“lest we be scattered”) and returns in verse 9, binding the account together. Elsewhere the verb describes God’s judgment in dispersing His disobedient people among the nations, and His promise later to gather them.

verses.bibleText: Therefore is the name of it called Babel; because the LORD did there confound the language of all the earth: and from thence did the LORD scatter them abroad upon the face of all the earth.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The account closes by naming the place. “Therefore is the name of it called Babel; because the LORD did there confound the language of all the earth.” The builders wanted to make themselves a name, and they received one: Babel, a name forever linked with confusion.

In the language of Babylon itself, the city’s name was understood as Bab-ili, “gate of god.” That meaning matched the ambition of its temple towers, which were regarded as stairways between earth and heaven. The Hebrew narrator hears the name differently and links it with balal, “to confound.” This is wordplay; it does not offer a technical etymology. It is a pointed verdict. What Babylon proclaimed as the gate of heaven, God exposed as a place of confusion. Human religion that tries to climb to God by its own works ends in bewilderment.

The repetition of “all the earth” and “scatter them abroad” draws a frame around the verse and around the whole story, which began with “the whole earth” speaking one language (v. 1). The movement is complete: from one speech to many, from settling to scattering, from a self-made name to a name of reproach.

This narrative is presented as real history, the origin of the world’s many languages and peoples, and the rest of Scripture treats it so. The site of the original tower has not been identified, though Babylon’s later great temple tower may have stood on or near it, and ancient Mesopotamia preserved a long tradition of building such towers. Faith rests on the testimony of the inspired word, which the details of the account consistently support.

Babylon now enters the Bible as a symbol. Throughout Scripture it stands for human pride organized against God: the power that carried Judah captive (2 Kings 25), the kingdom whose king exalted himself (Daniel 4:30), and finally the end-time “Babylon the great” of Revelation, a system of religious confusion that makes the nations drink its wine (Revelation 14:8; 17:5). The final call to God’s people is to come out of Babylon (Revelation 18:4). Against every Babel, God sets His own city, “which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God” (Hebrews 11:10).

wordNotes.explanation: The Hebrew name for Babylon, the same word used in Genesis 10:10 for the first city of Nimrod’s kingdom. Babylonians understood it as “gate of god”; the narrator connects its sound with balal, “confound.” Babel later becomes the name of the empire that destroyed Jerusalem and the prophetic symbol of end-time apostasy.

The verb means to mix or mingle, used of flour mixed with oil in offerings, and here of language mixed so that it can no longer serve communication. The narrator uses it to give the name Babel its true meaning in God’s eyes: confusion.

verses.bibleText: These are the generations of Shem: Shem was an hundred years old, and begat Arphaxad two years after the flood:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“These are the generations of Shem.” The familiar heading, toledot, marks a new section of Genesis, as it did for the heavens and the earth (2:4), Adam (5:1), Noah (6:9), and Noah’s sons (10:1). The narrator now returns to Shem, whose descendants were briefly listed in 10:21-31 before the story of Babel interrupted. The two lists serve different purposes. Chapter 10 spread outward to show how the peoples were related; this genealogy runs in a single straight line from Shem to Abram. It follows the pattern of Genesis 5, which traced ten generations from Adam to Noah, and now ten generations lead from Shem to Terah and his sons.

The placement is significant. Babel showed humanity seeking a name (shem) for itself. Immediately afterward comes the genealogy of a man whose very name is Shem, through whom God will give Abram a great name (12:2). Human striving for a name ends in confusion; God’s quiet preservation of a chosen line leads toward blessing.

Shem “was an hundred years old, and begat Arphaxad two years after the flood.” Since Noah was five hundred when he began to beget sons (5:32) and six hundred at the flood (7:6), this detail suggests Shem was not the eldest of the three, though he is listed first because of his place in the line of promise. Genesis repeatedly presents a younger son chosen ahead of an elder. The careful dating also ties this list to the flood as a fixed point in history, a real event in a real chronology.

These are individual persons, each with an age at a son’s birth and a span of years afterward, even though some of their names also became the names of peoples (10:22, 24). Through such ordinary-sounding records God was keeping His promise that the seed of the woman would come (3:15). The line runs on to Abraham, to David, and to Christ, whose genealogy in Luke passes back through these very names to “Sem, which was the son of Noe” (Luke 3:36).

wordNotes.term: תּוֹלְדֹת שֵׁם (toledot shem) — the generations of Shem
wordNotes.explanation: Toledot, from yalad, “to beget,” means “descendants” or “family history.” The formula opens each major section of Genesis and introduces what came from the named ancestor. Here it begins a linear genealogy that carries the line of blessing from Shem to Abram, matching the ten-generation pattern of Genesis 5.

Shem’s third-named son (10:22), through whom the line of promise continues. The name’s meaning is uncertain. Its final letters resemble Kesed, the root behind “Chaldees,” though any connection is uncertain. Luke spells it “Arphaxad,” following the Greek Old Testament.

verses.bibleText: And Shem lived after he begat Arphaxad five hundred years, and begat sons and daughters.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Shem lived after he begat Arphaxad five hundred years, and begat sons and daughters.” The verse sets the pattern repeated through verse 25: an age at the birth of the son in the chosen line, the years lived afterward, and a note that other children were born. Unlike Genesis 5, this list neither adds up a total lifespan nor ends each entry with “and he died.”

The totals are easy to calculate; Shem reached six hundred years. On the figures of the Hebrew text, he lived on for about a century and a half after Abram’s birth. The omission of the death refrain gives the list a forward-looking tone, as though the stress falls on continuity of life and witness. Shem, who had seen the world before the flood, could pass on the knowledge of the true God to generation after generation.

wordNotes.term: בָּנִים וּבָנוֹת (banim uvanot) — sons and daughters
wordNotes.explanation: A recurring phrase in the genealogies of Genesis 5 and 11 that reminds the reader of other children not named. Only the son through whom the chosen line continues is singled out. The phrase also shows God’s blessing of fruitfulness at work after the flood.

verses.bibleText: And Arphaxad lived five and thirty years, and begat Salah:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Arphaxad lived five and thirty years, and begat Salah.” The ages at which fathers have sons fall sharply after the flood. Before the flood the patriarchs became fathers of the named son anywhere between sixty-five and one hundred eighty-seven years; from Arphaxad onward the figures settle around thirty. The shift marks a new stage of human history, closer to the conditions of later times.

The Greek Old Testament inserts an additional name, Cainan, between Arphaxad and Salah, and Luke’s genealogy of Jesus includes him (Luke 3:36). Biblical genealogies often abbreviate a line, as comparisons within Scripture show (compare Ezra 7:1-5 with 1 Chronicles 6:3-14). The list remains a trustworthy record of descent, though not every reckoning of years before Abram can be fixed with complete precision.

wordNotes.explanation: The name likely means “sprout” or “one sent forth.” Luke follows the Greek spelling, Sala. Salah also appears in the Table of Nations as the link between Arphaxad and Eber.

verses.bibleText: And Arphaxad lived after he begat Salah four hundred and three years, and begat sons and daughters.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Arphaxad lived after he begat Salah four hundred and three years.” His total of four hundred thirty-eight years is far below Noah’s nine hundred fifty (9:29) and below Shem’s six hundred.

The decline in human lifespan begins visibly with him. Genesis records the change without explaining it, though the altered world after the flood and the new permission to eat flesh (9:3) belong to the same transition. Each new generation stood a little further from the strength with which the race was first made.

wordNotes.explanation: From chayah, “to live.” The verb opens each entry of the genealogy. Here, unlike Genesis 5, the entries close without the refrain “and he died,” keeping attention on life passed down.

verses.bibleText: And Salah lived thirty years, and begat Eber:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Salah lived thirty years, and begat Eber.” Eber holds a special place among these names. In the Table of Nations Shem is introduced as “the father of all the children of Eber” (10:21), even though Eber was Shem’s great-grandson. The name stands behind the word “Hebrew,” first applied to Abram in Genesis 14:13. Eber is therefore remembered as the ancestor whose name would mark the people of God. Balaam’s oracle later speaks of ships afflicting Eber, a poetic way of naming the Hebrews and their kin (Numbers 24:24).

The name is related to the idea of crossing over or passing beyond. Whether or not Eber’s family intended any such meaning, his descendant Abram would cross the Euphrates at God’s call and become a sojourner in a land not his own.

wordNotes.explanation: The name is related to ‘avar, “to pass over, cross,” and to ‘ever, “region beyond.” The gentilic ‘ivri, “Hebrew,” is linked with it. Joshua recalls that Israel’s fathers dwelt “on the other side of the flood” (the Euphrates), using the same word.

verses.bibleText: And Salah lived after he begat Eber four hundred and three years, and begat sons and daughters.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Salah lived after he begat Eber four hundred and three years.” Salah’s total of four hundred thirty-three years almost matches his father’s.

The list moves on without comment. Yet each line is a reminder that God was keeping the chosen family alive through the generations after the flood, as He had promised Noah (9:9-11), and that His purposes advance through ordinary births and passing years.

wordNotes.explanation: A causative form of yalad, “to bear, beget.” Repeated through the genealogy, it stresses fatherhood and the unbroken transmission of the line from one generation to the next.

verses.bibleText: And Eber lived four and thirty years, and begat Peleg:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Eber lived four and thirty years, and begat Peleg.” Peleg stands at the centre of the ten names from Shem to Terah, and his name links the genealogy to the Babel account. Genesis 10:25 explains that he was so named “for in his days was the earth divided.” The most natural reading connects that division with the dispersion of peoples after the confusion of tongues. Peleg’s birth thus helps locate Babel in time, a century or so after the flood according to the Hebrew figures.

His brother Joktan became the ancestor of Arabian tribes (10:26-30), but the chosen line runs through Peleg. While the nations were being divided, God was preserving the family through which He would one day bless them all.

wordNotes.explanation: The noun peleg means “channel” or “division,” and the related verb palag means “to divide.” Genesis 10:25 explains the name with niflegah, “was divided.” David uses the verb when he prays that God would divide the tongues of the wicked, a likely echo of Babel.

verses.bibleText: And Eber lived after he begat Peleg four hundred and thirty years, and begat sons and daughters.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Eber lived after he begat Peleg four hundred and thirty years.” Eber’s total of four hundred sixty-four years is the longest among Shem’s descendants in this list. On the Hebrew figures he lived on into the days of Abraham and beyond.

The ancestor whose name the Hebrews would bear could bear witness to the generations who came after him, linking Abram’s family to the faith preserved since the flood.

wordNotes.explanation: The ordinary word for a year, used throughout the genealogies with precise numbers. The exact figures present these men as historical persons in a real chronology, distinct from the vast symbolic reigns of Mesopotamian king lists.

verses.bibleText: And Peleg lived thirty years, and begat Reu:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Peleg lived thirty years, and begat Reu.” Reu’s name probably means “friend” or “companion,” perhaps a shortened form of a name such as Reuel, “friend of God” (Exodus 2:18).

With Reu begins the second half of the genealogy, the five names after Peleg that are not listed in chapter 10, leading on toward Terah.

wordNotes.explanation: Probably related to rea‘, “friend, companion.” Luke gives the Greek form Ragau. The meaning may echo names that confess friendship with God.

verses.bibleText: And Peleg lived after he begat Reu two hundred and nine years, and begat sons and daughters.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Peleg lived after he begat Reu two hundred and nine years.” The figure marks a striking drop. Peleg reached only two hundred thirty-nine years, little more than half the age of his father Eber. The sharp fall comes in the generation “in whose days the earth was divided,” as though the scattering after Babel coincided with a further step down in human vitality.

On the Hebrew reckoning Peleg died before Noah himself, who outlived several of his descendants. Sin’s consequences were working out in the human frame, generation by generation, just as God had warned (2:17).

wordNotes.term: תֵּשַׁע שָׁנִים וּמָאתַיִם שָׁנָה (tesha‘ shanim umatayim shanah) — two hundred and nine years
wordNotes.explanation: The dual form of me’ah, “hundred.” From Peleg on, the remaining years of each patriarch fall to around two hundred, a level that continues until a further drop with Nahor.

verses.bibleText: And Reu lived two and thirty years, and begat Serug:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Reu lived two and thirty years, and begat Serug.” The pattern of fathering the next son around age thirty holds steady, and the record passes on without a single remarkable deed.

Each line is brief, but each represents a household through which God kept the knowledge of Himself alive while much of the world was drifting into idolatry. Faithfulness across generations seldom draws attention; it is handed on in homes, from parents to children, as the Psalmist says: “One generation shall praise thy works to another” (Psalm 145:4).

wordNotes.explanation: The name may relate to sarag, “to intertwine,” possibly meaning “branch” or “tendril.” A town called Sarugi near Haran preserves the same name, linking the family with that region.

verses.bibleText: And Reu lived after he begat Serug two hundred and seven years, and begat sons and daughters.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Reu lived after he begat Serug two hundred and seven years.” Reu’s total of two hundred thirty-nine years exactly matches his father Peleg’s. The plateau at this level shows that the decline in lifespan was not steady in every generation but came in stages, with Peleg and later Nahor marking the steepest falls.

Moses would eventually write that the days of mortal life are seventy years, or eighty by reason of strength (Psalm 90:10).

wordNotes.term: שֶׁבַע שָׁנִים וּמָאתַיִם שָׁנָה (sheva‘ shanim umatayim shanah) — two hundred and seven years
wordNotes.explanation: The numbers in the genealogy are written out in full as words. Such exact, uneven figures suit a record of real lives, unlike the rounded totals of legend.

verses.bibleText: And Serug lived thirty years, and begat Nahor:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Serug lived thirty years, and begat Nahor.” This Nahor is the grandfather of Abram, and his name will be given again to one of Terah’s sons (v. 26). Repeating a grandfather’s name was a natural way to honour the family line.

The town of Nahor near Haran (24:10) suggests that the family was associated with northern Mesopotamia.

wordNotes.explanation: The name is often linked with nachar, “to snort” or “breathe heavily,” though its meaning is uncertain. The city of Nahor, home of Rebekah’s family, carries the same name.

verses.bibleText: And Serug lived after he begat Nahor two hundred years, and begat sons and daughters.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Serug lived after he begat Nahor two hundred years.” Serug lived two hundred thirty years in all. Each generation in this second half of the list repeats almost the same span, a steady rhythm of continuity before the sudden shortening that comes with Nahor.

These spans still far exceed ordinary lives today, and they meant that several generations lived side by side for centuries. A grandson could hear the history of the flood from men who had heard it from Noah’s own sons. God provided for His truth to be handed down by living witnesses long before it was written in Scripture.

wordNotes.term: אַחֲרֵי הוֹלִידוֹ (acharei holido) — after he begat
wordNotes.explanation: A recurring phrase dividing each life into the years before and after the birth of the son in the chosen line, keeping that line central.

verses.bibleText: And Nahor lived nine and twenty years, and begat Terah:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Nahor lived nine and twenty years, and begat Terah.” Nahor fathered the next son at the youngest age in the list.

With Terah the genealogy approaches its goal. Terah’s household served other gods in Ur (Joshua 24:2), so the line of promise was not kept pure by the merit of each member. It was carried forward by the faithfulness of God, who called Abram out of an idolatrous family.

wordNotes.explanation: The meaning is uncertain. Some connect it with yareach, “moon,” which would fit the moon worship centred at Ur and Haran, but the link is not proven. Joshua names Terah as a worshipper of other gods.

verses.bibleText: And Nahor lived after he begat Terah an hundred and nineteen years, and begat sons and daughters.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Nahor lived after he begat Terah an hundred and nineteen years.” Nahor’s total of one hundred forty-eight years is the shortest so far, less than half that of his own father Serug. Within ten generations human life has fallen from six hundred years to well under two hundred. Scripture does not give a single explanation. The changed world after the flood, the move from a diet of plants to one including flesh (9:3), and increasing distance from the life-giving tree of the garden (3:22) all belong to the picture.

What the numbers show beyond doubt is that death, the penalty of sin, was pressing ever more heavily upon the race. God’s gift of life is precious and fragile, and the care of the body He made remains a matter of faithfulness.

wordNotes.term: תְּשַׁע־עֶשְׂרֵה שָׁנָה וּמְאַת שָׁנָה (tesha‘-‘esreh shanah ume’at shanah) — an hundred and nineteen years
wordNotes.explanation: The figure leaves Nahor with one hundred forty-eight years in total. Abraham will live one hundred seventy-five years, and Jacob one hundred forty-seven, showing the patriarchal age now settled near this range.

verses.bibleText: And Terah lived seventy years, and begat Abram, Nahor, and Haran.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Terah lived seventy years, and begat Abram, Nahor, and Haran.” Like Genesis 5:32, which names Noah’s three sons together, the genealogy ends by branching into three. The wording does not require that all three were born when Terah was seventy, as if they were triplets. It marks the age at which Terah began to have sons and then names all three together.

Other passages show that Abram was born considerably later. Terah died in Haran at two hundred five (11:32). Abram left Haran at seventy-five (12:4), and Stephen states that he did so after his father’s death (Acts 7:4). Abram must therefore have been born when Terah was about one hundred thirty. He is named first because of his importance in God’s plan. He was not the firstborn. Genesis often lists the chosen son ahead of his brothers in this way (compare Shem in 5:32), and repeatedly shows God choosing a younger son over an elder.

By these figures Abram was born about three hundred fifty years after the flood. Noah had died shortly before, and Shem was still living. The knowledge of the true God, carried by an unbroken line from Adam through Noah and Shem, was available to Abram’s generation, even though Terah’s own household had turned to other gods.

The name Abram means “exalted father,” an honourable name already, though it would gain new meaning when God changed it to Abraham, “father of a multitude” (17:5). Here, at the close of the genealogy, the reader meets him simply as one of three sons. Nothing in him explains why he should be chosen. The next verses will show his family and his wife’s barrenness, and chapter 12 will reveal that his story begins with God’s call and God’s promise. The long line from Shem has narrowed to one man, and through that man, God will bring blessing to all the families of the earth (12:3; Galatians 3:8, 16).

wordNotes.explanation: Probably “exalted father” or “the father is exalted.” God later lengthens it to Abraham, linked by sound with “father of a multitude of nations.” The new name expresses what God will make of him; the original name reflects only what his family hoped for.

The age at which Terah began to beget his sons. Read with Genesis 11:32, Genesis 12:4, and Acts 7:4, it shows that the three sons were born over a span of years and that Abram, though listed first, was born when Terah was about one hundred thirty.

verses.bibleText: Now these are the generations of Terah: Terah begat Abram, Nahor, and Haran; and Haran begat Lot.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Now these are the generations of Terah.” A new toledot heading opens the section that will run through the life of Abraham to 25:11. Up to this point Genesis has told the story of all humanity. From here on the narrative narrows to one family, and other nations will appear chiefly as they touch the people of God. The heading names Terah as the ancestor, yet the story that follows centres on his son. It is the account of what came from Terah, and above all of Abram.

The verse repeats the three sons from verse 26 and adds one more name: “Haran begat Lot.” Lot is introduced at once because he will travel with Abram, share his early journeys, separate from him toward Sodom (13:11-12), and become the ancestor of Moab and Ammon (19:36-38). His presence in the household explains much that follows. Since his father died young, Lot attached himself to his uncle Abram, and his choices will repeatedly test Abram’s faith and generosity.

The family introduced here is ordinary in many ways. It has births and deaths, marriages and disappointments, and a father whose religion was mixed with idolatry (Joshua 24:2). God did not choose a model household to carry His promise. He called a man out of such a household and shaped him by grace. The New Testament presents Abraham as the father of all who believe, not because his family was worthy, but because he “believed God, and it was counted unto him for righteousness” (Romans 4:3).

wordNotes.term: תּוֹלְדֹת תֶּרַח (toledot Terach) — the generations of Terah
wordNotes.explanation: The sixth toledot heading in Genesis. Like the others, it names the ancestor and then tells what came from him. Although Terah is named, the account that follows is the story of Abram, since that is what came of Terah’s line.

The name may relate to lut, “to wrap, cover,” perhaps meaning “covering” or “hidden.” Lot is Haran’s son and Abram’s nephew; Peter later calls him “just Lot,” troubled by the wickedness around him in Sodom.

verses.bibleText: And Haran died before his father Terah in the land of his nativity, in Ur of the Chaldees.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Haran died before his father Terah.” The Hebrew phrase is literally “upon the face of Terah his father,” meaning that Haran died during his father’s lifetime and perhaps in his presence. Abel had died long before Adam, but this is the first time Genesis expressly notes that a son died while his father still lived. The order of nature was reversed, and the grief of such a loss would mark the family that set out from Ur. The early death also explains why Lot was later in his uncle’s care.

“In the land of his nativity, in Ur of the Chaldees.” Ur was the family’s home. The great city of Ur in southern Mesopotamia, on the Euphrates near the Persian Gulf, has been excavated extensively. In the early second millennium BC it was a wealthy and highly developed city, with two-storey houses, schools, trade, and a towering temple tower dedicated to the moon god. Abram did not grow up as an ignorant nomad. He knew the comforts of a cultured city and its polytheistic worship. Some have proposed a northern Ur nearer Haran, but the southern city remains the most likely identification, and the route described in verse 31 suits it.

The term “Chaldees” refers to the people who later gave their name to southern Babylonia. Moses may have used it to identify the place for later readers, much as a modern writer might give a city’s current name. God reminds Abram, “I am the LORD that brought thee out of Ur of the Chaldees” (15:7), and Nehemiah repeats the same confession (Nehemiah 9:7). The call that began in Ur was God’s initiative from the start.

wordNotes.term: עַל־פְּנֵי תֶּרַח אָבִיו (‘al-penei Terach aviv) — before his father Terah
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “upon the face of Terah his father.” The idiom means “in the lifetime of” or “in the presence of.” A similar idiom is used when Nadab and Abihu ministered and died while Aaron their father lived.

wordNotes.term: אוּר כַּשְׂדִּים (’Ur Kasdim) — Ur of the Chaldees
wordNotes.explanation: The Kasdim are the Chaldeans, a people later dominant in southern Babylonia. The Greek Old Testament renders the phrase “the land of the Chaldeans.” Stephen describes Abram’s first call as coming to him in Mesopotamia, before he lived in Haran.

verses.bibleText: And Abram and Nahor took them wives: the name of Abram's wife was Sarai; and the name of Nahor's wife, Milcah, the daughter of Haran, the father of Milcah, and the father of Iscah.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Abram and Nahor took them wives.” The two surviving brothers marry. Abram’s wife is Sarai, and Nahor’s is Milcah, “the daughter of Haran.” Nahor thus married his niece, the daughter of his dead brother. Abram’s marriage was also within the family. Later he explains that Sarai “is the daughter of my father, but not the daughter of my mother” (20:12), making her his half-sister. Such close marriages were still customary in that age, though the law given through Moses would later forbid them (Leviticus 18:9). Genesis records the custom honestly, and it becomes the background for Abram’s half-truth when he calls Sarai his sister in Egypt and Gerar (12:13; 20:2).

The verse carefully gives Milcah’s ancestry but offers none for Sarai beyond her marriage. Milcah will bear eight sons to Nahor (22:20-23), and through one of them she becomes the grandmother of Rebekah, Isaac’s wife (24:15). The detail sets up the contrast of the next verse. One wife in the family is fruitful; the other, the wife of the man God will call, has no child.

Iscah is mentioned only here. Ancient Jewish tradition identified her with Sarai, but Genesis 20:12 makes Sarai Terah’s daughter, which rules out Iscah, Haran’s daughter. Nothing more is known of her. Her name simply completes the record of Haran’s children, preserving a memory that the reader is not told to interpret further.

wordNotes.explanation: Probably an old form meaning “princess.” God later changes it to Sarah (also “princess”), confirming that kings of peoples would come from her. The name change, like Abram’s, marks God’s promise reshaping her identity.
Related to malkah, “queen.” She is Haran’s daughter and Nahor’s wife, mother of Bethuel and grandmother of Rebekah. Her fruitfulness stands in deliberate contrast with Sarai’s barrenness.

verses.bibleText: But Sarai was barren; she had no child.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“But Sarai was barren; she had no child.” The statement is short, but it hangs over the whole story that follows. The narrator says it twice in different words, as if to leave no doubt: barren, and without a child. In the ancient world childlessness was a deep sorrow and often a social disgrace, and for a family line it meant the end of the name.

The placement is deliberate. The genealogy has just traced an unbroken line of fathers and sons from Shem to Terah, each one begetting the next. Now the line reaches Abram and stops at a closed womb. Humanly speaking, the promise has nowhere to go. Yet in the very next chapter God will promise Abram, “I will make of thee a great nation” (12:2). The barrenness is the stage on which God will display that the promise depends on His power alone.

This pattern runs through Scripture. Rebekah (25:21), Rachel (29:31), Manoah’s wife (Judges 13:2), Hannah (1 Samuel 1:2), and Elisabeth (Luke 1:7) were all barren before God gave them sons who carried His purposes forward. Each time, life came where nature offered none, so that no one could boast. Paul draws the lesson: Abraham considered “the deadness of Sarah’s womb” and still “staggered not at the promise of God through unbelief” (Romans 4:19-20). Hebrews adds that Sarah herself received strength to conceive “because she judged him faithful who had promised” (Hebrews 11:11).

The line of promise thus runs through human impossibility. It points toward the greatest birth of all, when a virgin conceived by the power of the Most High, because “with God nothing shall be impossible” (Luke 1:35-37). Those who feel their lives are barren of fruit may take courage. God often begins His work exactly where human resources end.

wordNotes.explanation: An adjective for a woman unable to bear children. It describes Rebekah, Rachel, and Manoah’s wife before God intervened, and Isaiah uses it of desolate Zion, called to sing because her children will be many. In each case barrenness becomes the setting for God’s gift.

wordNotes.term: אֵין לָהּ וָלָד (’ein lah valad) — she had no child
wordNotes.explanation: Valad, “child, offspring,” is a rare word related to yalad, “to bear.” The repetition after “barren” underlines the human impossibility that God’s promise will overcome.

verses.bibleText: And Terah took Abram his son, and Lot the son of Haran his son's son, and Sarai his daughter in law, his son Abram's wife; and they went forth with them from Ur of the Chaldees, to go into the land of Canaan; and they came unto Haran, and dwelt there.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Terah took Abram his son, and Lot the son of Haran his son’s son, and Sarai his daughter in law.” The household sets out from Ur of the Chaldees “to go into the land of Canaan.” Canaan was the destination from the beginning. The verse names Terah as leader, which fits the customs of the time; a father remained head of the household, and it would have been unseemly to say that a son led his father.

Other Scriptures show that the call came to Abram. Stephen said, “The God of glory appeared unto our father Abraham, when he was in Mesopotamia, before he dwelt in Charran,” and told him to leave his country and kindred (Acts 7:2-3). God Himself later said He had brought Abram out of Ur (15:7). Abram’s call came in two stages. In Ur he was called to leave his homeland, and Terah and Lot chose to go with him; in Haran, after Terah’s death, he was called to leave his father’s house and go on alone with his own household (12:1-4). Nahor and Milcah are not mentioned as leaving Ur, though they appear later in the region of Haran (24:10).

The route followed the arc of fertile land up the Euphrates, then westward and south into Canaan, since a direct crossing of the Arabian desert was impossible with flocks and herds. Haran lay on the Balikh River in northern Mesopotamia, a busy crossroads on the trade routes, roughly halfway to Canaan.

Then comes a sobering phrase: “they came unto Haran, and dwelt there.” The same verb described the builders who “dwelt” in Shinar (v. 2). The household that set out for Canaan stopped short. Whether because of Terah’s age, the attraction of good pasture, or other reasons, the journey paused for years. Delay in obeying God is common among those who have begun to follow Him. The writer of Hebrews celebrates Abraham’s faith, that he went out “not knowing whither he went” (Hebrews 11:8). That faith had to be renewed after the halt at Haran, and God graciously renewed His call.

wordNotes.explanation: A city in northern Mesopotamia on the Balikh River, spelled differently in Hebrew from the name of Abram’s brother (Haran). Its name likely meant “road” or “crossroads,” fitting its place on the trade routes. Jacob later fled there to Laban, and Stephen calls it Charran.

wordNotes.term: וַיֵּשְׁבוּ שָׁם (vayyeshvu sham) — and dwelt there
wordNotes.explanation: The same words used of the builders who settled in Shinar (v. 2). Both groups set out and then settled. The builders settled in defiance of God; Terah’s household settled short of the goal God had set.

verses.bibleText: And the days of Terah were two hundred and five years: and Terah died in Haran.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And the days of Terah were two hundred and five years: and Terah died in Haran.” The chapter ends with a death short of the promised land. Terah set out for Canaan but never reached it. The phrase “and he died” has been absent through the genealogy of Shem; it returns here as a solemn close, bringing Terah’s part of the story to an end.

Stephen explains that it was after Terah’s death that God moved Abram from Haran into Canaan (Acts 7:4). Abram seems to have remained in Haran during his father’s last years, perhaps out of filial care. When Terah died, Abram, Sarai, and Lot went on. Nahor’s branch of the family stayed in the region, and generations later Abraham’s servant and Jacob would return there to find wives from that household (24:10; 28:2). Remaining in Haran kept that branch of the family outside the land of promise.

Terah’s death in Haran is a reminder that setting out is not the same as arriving. Many begin a journey toward God’s promise and stop at a comfortable halfway place. Moses too died within sight of Canaan without entering it (Deuteronomy 34:4). The faithful of every age have died as pilgrims, “not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off” (Hebrews 11:13). Their hope looks beyond the grave to the resurrection, when God will bring His people into the better country He has prepared (Hebrews 11:16, 39-40).

The chapter that began with humanity united in pride ends with one family in mourning, a barren wife, and an unfinished journey. From Babel came only scattering. From this small household in Haran, God will begin the work of gathering the nations to Himself. The next verse begins, “Now the LORD had said unto Abram, Get thee out” (12:1). Where human plans have stalled, the word of God takes up the story.

wordNotes.term: וַיָּמָת תֶּרַח בְּחָרָן (vayyamot Terach becharan) — and Terah died in Haran
wordNotes.explanation: The death formula, absent from the genealogy of Shem, returns at the close of Terah’s life. In Scripture death is the cessation of life, the sleep from which God’s people await resurrection. Terah’s death outside Canaan marks the point at which Abram’s own journey of faith begins.

teachingNotes.openingQuestion: Where do people today look for a lasting name, security, and unity, and what happens when they seek these things apart from God?
teachingNotes.mainPoint: Human self-exaltation ends in confusion and scattering, but God, who comes down to judge pride, also preserves a line through which He will give a true name and bless the scattered nations.
discussionQuestions: How does the builders’ fear of being scattered reveal what they did not trust about God?
Why does the narrator stress that the LORD had to come down to see a tower meant to reach heaven?
In what ways was the confusion of languages an act of mercy as well as judgment?
What does the long genealogy from Shem to Terah teach about God’s faithfulness across generations?
Why might Genesis mention Sarai’s barrenness immediately before God’s great promise to Abram?
commonMisunderstandings: The text does not condemn cities, building skill, or technology as such; it exposes the pride and unbelief that drove this particular project.
The LORD’s coming down does not imply that God was ignorant; it shows that He examines human deeds before He acts in judgment.
Terah being seventy when he “begat Abram, Nahor, and Haran” does not mean the three were born together or that Abram was the eldest.
teachingNotes.emphasis: Hold the two halves of the chapter together: the nations scattered by pride at Babel are the very nations God will bless through the obscure, childless family introduced at the end.
teachingNotes.closingAppeal: Lay down every effort to build a name apart from God, and receive the name, security, and fellowship He gives to those who follow His call.

evangelisticNotes.mainDoctrinalTheme: Salvation comes by God’s descent in grace rather than human ascent by achievement; the God who scattered proud Babel gathers a people from every tongue through Christ.
flow: At Babel humanity tried to reach heaven and secure its own name by its own work.
The LORD came down, judged their pride, and scattered them, restraining evil from ripening as before the flood.
God then chose one family, promising a great name and blessing for all the families of the earth.
In Christ, God came down fully, and at Pentecost the gospel was heard in many tongues.
The final message calls people out of every modern Babel into the worship of the Creator.
simpleIllustrations: A ladder built from the ground can never reach the sky; a rope let down from above is the only way up.
A building crew that suddenly cannot understand one another must stop work, however grand the plans.
evangelisticNotes.appealQuestion: Will you stop building your own way to heaven and receive the way God has opened by coming down in Jesus Christ?
cautions: Do not use the Babel account to justify ethnic pride or contempt for other peoples; all nations share one origin and are objects of God’s blessing.
Do not reduce the story to a lesson against architecture or progress; its target is pride and independence from God.
When applying the Babylon theme to the last days, speak of systems of confusion, not of the sincere people within them.

reflectionQuestions: What am I building in order to make a name for myself, and would I be content if God never let it be finished?
Where do my fears of being overlooked or unsettled push me to rely on my own plans rather than God’s word?
How has God mercifully interrupted my projects when they were leading me away from Him?
Who in my family line or spiritual heritage passed on the knowledge of God to me, and how am I passing it on?
What barren place in my life might God be preparing as the setting for His promise?
